Sourdough

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Bread made by fermentation of dough
For the gold rush miners, see Sourdough (miner).
This article needs additional citations.
Sourdough
TypeInfoboxTypeBread
Place of originAncient Egypt

Sourdough is a type of bread that uses the fermentation by naturally occurring yeast and lactobacillus bacteria to raise the dough.[1] In addition to leavening the bread, the fermentation process produces lactic acid, which gives the bread its distinctive sour taste.[2]

Contents

  • 1 History

History

[edit]

Sourdough is one of the oldest forms of grain leavening.[3] It is believed to have originated in Ancient Egypt around 1500 BC.

Gold rush

[edit]
A prospector in 1898

Sourdough was the main bread in Northern California during the California Gold Rush, and it remains a part of the culture of San Francisco.

Chemistry

[edit]

A sourdough starter is a stable culture of lactic acid bacteria and yeast in a mixture of flour and water.
